title: Learning Multi-Agent Coordination via Sheaf-ADMM
one_liner: Give each agent a local optimization problem and force neighboring agents to agree only on the parts that should match, then train the whole coordination process end to end.
lead: This paper builds multi-agent coordination as differentiable optimization. Each agent sees only a local view, solves a convex subproblem, and exchanges agreement constraints with neighbors through ADMM. A sheaf specifies exactly which parts of neighboring solutions must agree, so the system can learn partial or structured consensus instead of forcing every agent to match on everything.

problem.h2: Why local views are not enough by themselves
paras: In many coordination problems, each agent sees only a piece of the full input. A single local view may be insufficient for a correct global decision because important constraints cross agent boundaries.

Standard message-passing systems often learn opaque hidden states. They can solve the task, but it is hard to inspect what each agent is optimizing or why the agents agree. This paper uses explicit optimization states so that coordination is both trainable and analyzable.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Turn coordination into repeated local optimization plus explicit agreement steps so that agents learn from local evidence while still satisfying global consistency constraints.

panels.title: 1. Each agent sees only part of the task
panels.viz_args: Local views overlap, but no agent sees the whole problem
panels.caption: Local information is incomplete, so isolated solutions are often inconsistent.

panels.title: 2. Independent local solutions clash
panels.caption: Agents can each solve their own local problem and still disagree on the shared parts.

panels.title: 3. Sheaf rules specify what must match
panels.viz_args: Neighbor pairs agree only on selected components
panels.caption: The coordination rule is structured because not every part of every local solution should be identical.

panels.title: 4. ADMM alternates local solve and agreement
panels.viz_args: Local update, consensus update, dual update
panels.caption: The method repeatedly reduces local error and shared inconsistency.

panels.title: 5. A coherent global answer emerges
panels.caption: Coordination succeeds because local solutions are nudged toward compatibility until the shared constraints are satisfied.

steps.b: Split the input into overlapping local views
steps.text: Assign each agent a local slice of the problem so that every agent solves a smaller optimization task.
A neural encoder maps the local observation into the numeric settings of that agent's convex subproblem so that the optimization reflects the input.
Each agent computes its current best local solution based on its own objective and the current coordination terms.
ADMM updates the consensus and dual variables so that overlapping agents reduce disagreement on the components that should match.
Train the encoders end to end because error signals through the optimization steps tell each encoder how to produce better local objectives.

paras: The paper changes coordination from opaque message passing into explicit local optimization with structured agreement constraints.

hidden.name: How far the local solutions are from global consistency
paras: At any iteration, each agent has a local candidate solution, but the system does not directly observe how close the collection is to a globally valid answer until agreement is checked. The important hidden quantity is the mismatch on shared components across neighboring agents.
ADMM exposes that mismatch through primal, consensus, and dual variables. That is useful because you can inspect where coordination is failing instead of only seeing the final error.

heat.caption: Darker means larger or more important disagreement that the coordination process still needs to reduce.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the remaining mismatch between local answers on the pieces they share.
The method tracks explicit coordination residuals so that structured consensus can be learned and inspected.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: separate local solving from global agreement
paras: The method works because each agent can focus on a small tractable subproblem while ADMM handles the cross-agent consistency. That division is useful because local evidence can be processed where it is strongest, and only the overlapping components need coordination.

The sheaf matters because different tasks need different notions of agreement. Some neighbors should match on one variable but not another. Structured agreement avoids overconstraining the system, so agents can keep useful local freedom while still producing a coherent global result.

stages.s: Each agent solves its local convex problem

math.words: A simple view is that each agent minimizes its local objective plus a penalty for disagreeing with the shared consensus variable. That penalty matters because it pushes neighboring agents toward compatible local solutions during repeated updates.
symbols: the objective minimized by agent i at one update
how well agent i solves its own local subproblem
the strength of the coordination pressure
how far agent i is from the current shared consensus on overlapping components

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Two neighboring Sudoku agents both decide a shared cell value.
Agent A prefers 7 with local loss 1.
Consensus currently says 5, so disagreement is 2 and penalty strength is 3.
The large disagreement cost pushes the next update toward a value closer to the shared choice.

math.note: The full ADMM update includes separate primal, consensus, and dual steps, but this summary captures the role of disagreement penalties in driving coordination.

charts.title: Independent or loosely coordinated agents
charts.note: Weakly structured coordination trails because local views are insufficient without explicit consistency updates.

charts.title: Sheaf-ADMM coordination
charts.note: The optimization-based system performs better because local solving and structured agreement are both enforced directly. The values are illustrative summaries of the reported trend.

items.b: The local subproblem may be a poor abstraction.
items.html: If the convex local objective does not capture what the task really needs, repeated coordination cannot fully repair the mismatch because each agent is solving the wrong local problem.
If the sheaf specifies too much agreement, agents lose needed flexibility, and if it specifies too little agreement, local solutions remain inconsistent.
Training through many ADMM steps increases training cost because each step must be stored and differentiated.
The paper is useful because it exposes coordination state directly, which helps analysis and intervention during learning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small puzzle or routing task where each agent sees an overlapping local region and must agree with neighbors on shared variables. Implement one baseline with learned message passing and one system with explicit local objectives plus ADMM updates. Expose the consensus and dual variables at each step.

The demo should show that the optimization-based system reaches a higher valid-solution rate because disagreement is penalized directly instead of being left to an implicit learned communication channel. Visualize residual disagreement over updates so that the coordination process is observable.
demo.closing: The demo must prove that explicit agreement updates improve coordination because local views alone do not determine a coherent global answer.
